name.text: WAT 22.1: The Case That Ate Everything!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three functions that each pick an answer with one match statement.

How this works in Python

Java 14 gave you the arrow switch, and you have written it a hundred times.

String describe(int code) {
    return switch (code) {
        case 0 -> "idle";
        case 1, 2 -> "running";
        case 3 -> "stopping";
        default -> "unknown code " + code;
    };
}

Python 3.10 added the same shape under the name structural pattern matching, spelled match and case. Most Python material on the internet is older than it, which is why you have not seen it yet.

match code:
    case 0:
        return "idle"
    case 1 | 2:
        return "running"
    case 3:
        return "stopping"
    case other:
        return f"unknown code {other}"

Python tries the cases from the top and stops at the first one that fits. There is no fallthrough and no break, so the body runs and the whole statement ends.

A statement, not an expression

Here is the first difference that will bite you. The Java arrow switch is an expression, so it produces a value and you return the whole thing. A Python match is a statement, and a statement produces nothing. Each case body has to return or assign for itself, which is why every branch above carries its own return.

match and case are soft keywords. A variable called match elsewhere in your program keeps working, because Python decides what the word means from where it sits on the line.

Four kinds of pattern

A literal pattern such as case 0: or case "stop": compares the subject with ==. That is the closest thing to a Java case label.

An alternative puts several patterns in one case, separated by |. Where Java writes case 1, 2 ->, Python writes case 1 | 2:. Reach for it whenever two values share a body.

The wildcard case _: matches anything and binds nothing. It reads like Java's default and behaves very differently in one respect. Java's switch over a sealed type refuses to compile when you miss a subtype. Python checks nothing at all, so a subject that fits no case falls off the end of the match and the statement does nothing. Inside a function that means a silent None comes back, which in a safety controller is a fault nobody reads.

A capture pattern is a bare name such as case other:. It matches anything, like the wildcard, and it also binds the subject to that name so the body can read it. Use it when the fallback needs to report what arrived.

The trap that eats your dispatch

Read this section twice, because it costs people whole afternoons. A bare name in a case is always a capture and never a comparison. It does not matter that the name already exists and holds the value you wanted to test against.

FAILED = Status.FAILED

match status:
    case FAILED:                 # not a comparison. This binds.
        return "tripped"

That case matches every status. It also rebinds FAILED to whatever came in, so the name you trusted now holds the subject.

The trap wears two faces. Put cases after the bare name and Python stops you at compile time, which is the kind day.

SyntaxError: name capture 'FAILED' makes remaining patterns unreachable

Put the bare name last and Python compiles it without a murmur, because the last case is allowed to match everything. Your dispatcher now answers "tripped" for a healthy sensor and no error is raised anywhere. The supplied broken_alert in the answer box is exactly that, and one of the tests runs it beside yours so you can watch it lie.

The fix is a dot

A dotted name is a different animal. It is a value pattern, and a value pattern compares.

case Status.FAILED:              # compares with ==
case Status.OK:

Python treats the dot as proof that you meant the thing on the right of it rather than a fresh variable. Enum members therefore belong inside a match, and loose module constants such as that FAILED do not. This is one more reason the enums topic told you to give a set of related constants a proper Enum.

Your task

The answer box opens with a supplied block holding Status, a module constant FAILED and the broken broken_alert. Leave every line of it alone. Write the three functions below it.

  • describe_code(code) takes a whole number. 0 gives "idle", 1 and 2 both give "running", and 3 gives "stopping". Anything else gives f"unknown code {code}", and the last case must bind the value to a name of your choosing rather than use case _.
  • alert(status) takes a Status member. Status.FAILED gives "trip", Status.OK gives "all good", and any other member gives "stale reading" through case _. This is the working version of broken_alert.
  • label(word) takes a string. "on" and "start" give "running". "off", "stop" and "halt" give "stopped". The empty string gives "no word given". Anything else gives "unrecognised".

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text exactly.

Rules
  • Do not write if, elif or else. The match statement picks the branch.
  • Compare an enum member with a dotted name. case Status.FAILED compares, and case FAILED binds a new variable and swallows the subject whole.
  • Put alternatives in one case with |. Do not repeat a body across two cases.
  • Leave the supplied block untouched, broken function and all. A hidden test calls it.
  • Annotate every signature, parameters and return alike.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

No AI. Type every character yourself. This tier builds the muscle, and a tool that types it for you skips the exercise.

question.answer:
from enum import Enum
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # Supplied. Do not change anything in this block. # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- class Status(Enum): OK = "OK" FAILED = "FAILED" STALE = "STALE"
FAILED = Status.FAILED
def broken_alert(status: Status) -> str: match status: case Status.STALE: return "stale reading" case FAILED: return f"tripped, and FAILED now means {FAILED.name}" # ---------------------------------------------------------------------- # End of the supplied block. # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
def describe_code(code: int) -> str: match code: case 0: return "idle" case 1 | 2: return "running" case 3: return "stopping" case other: return f"unknown code {other}"
def alert(status: Status) -> str: match status: case Status.FAILED: return "trip" case Status.OK: return "all good" case _: return "stale reading"
def label(word: str) -> str: match word: case "on" | "start": return "running" case "off" | "stop" | "halt": return "stopped" case "": return "no word given" case _: return "unrecognised"

expected.text: idle running running stopping unknown code 7 running running stopped stopped stopped no word given unrecognised

testcode.text: for status in (Status.FAILED, Status.OK, Status.STALE): print(f"{status.name}: yours says {alert(status)}, the broken one says {broken_alert(status)}")

expected.text: FAILED: yours says trip, the broken one says tripped, and FAILED now means FAILED OK: yours says all good, the broken one says tripped, and FAILED now means OK STALE: yours says stale reading, the broken one says stale reading

testcode.text:
import inspect
sources = {f.__name__: inspect.getsource(f) for f in (describe_code, alert, label)} for name, source in sources.items(): for line in source.splitlines(): head = line.strip() assert not head.startswith("if "), "rule broken: no if statement, the match picks the branch" assert not head.startswith("elif "), "rule broken: no elif, the match picks the branch" assert not head.startswith("else"), "rule broken: no else, the match picks the branch" assert "match " in source, "rule broken: every answer uses one match statement" assert "Status.FAILED" in sources["alert"], "rule broken: compare an enum with a dotted name" assert "case _" in sources["alert"], "rule broken: alert ends with case _" assert "case _" in sources["label"], "rule broken: label ends with case _" assert "case _" not in sources["describe_code"], "rule broken: the last case of describe_code binds a name" assert "|" in sources["label"], "rule broken: put alternatives in one case with |" assert "|" in sources["describe_code"], "rule broken: put alternatives in one case with |" assert sources["label"].count("case ") == 4, "rule broken: four cases, do not repeat a body" assert sources["describe_code"].count("case ") == 4, "rule broken: four cases, do not repeat a body" print(describe_code(-1), "|", describe_code(3)) print(alert(Status.STALE), "|", alert(Status.FAILED)) print(label("HALT"), "|", label("stop")) print(broken_alert(Status.OK))

expected.text: unknown code -1 | stopping stale reading | trip unrecognised | stopped tripped, and FAILED now means OK

name.text: WAT 22.2: Shape Up or Ship Out!

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three functions that read a list, a coordinate pair and a dict, each with one match statement.

How this works in Python

Java 21 lets a switch take a record apart in the case label, and when adds a condition.

switch (shape) {
    case Point(int x, int y) when x == y -> "on the diagonal at " + x;
    case Point(int x, int y) -> "at " + x + "," + y;
    default -> "not a point";
}

That is as far as Java goes. There is no case label for a List and none for a Map, so a two element list is still size() and two calls to get, with the bounds check written by hand.

if (samples.isEmpty()) return "no samples";
int first = samples.get(0);
if (first > 100) {
    return "spike at " + first + ", " + (samples.size() - 1) + " more";
}

Python matches a list and a dict as readily as it matches a record. Three tools do it, and the earlier tier of this topic gave you the rest of the statement.

Sequence patterns match by shape

match samples:
    case []:
        return "no samples"
    case [only]:
        return f"one sample: {only}"
    case [first, *rest]:
        return f"starts at {first}, {len(rest)} more"

Length and position decide. [] wants nothing, [only] wants exactly one item, and [a, b] wants exactly two. A name inside the brackets is a capture, so it binds the item sitting in that position.

A starred name soaks up whatever is left over, which is the same star you met when unpacking a tuple. [first, *rest] therefore matches a list of one item or a list of a hundred, and rest arrives as a list that is empty in the first of those two cases. The star can sit in the middle as well, so [first, *middle, last] is a legal pattern.

Two surprises live here. The square brackets describe a shape rather than a list, so a tuple matches case [x, y] as happily as a list does. And strings never match a sequence pattern at all, which stops the word "ab" passing itself off as a coordinate pair.

Mapping patterns match by key

match config:
    case {"mode": "auto", "limit": limit}:
        return f"auto up to {limit}"

That case wants a "mode" key holding "auto" and a "limit" key holding anything, and it binds the limit. Now the rule that catches everybody. A mapping pattern asks for a subset, so any other key in the dict is ignored and the case still fits. Sequence patterns demand the exact length and mapping patterns do not, and the two rules sit one page apart in your head.

The subset rule has a sharp edge. case {}: asks for no keys at all, so it matches every mapping including a full one. It does not mean "an empty dict". Put it anywhere except last and every case below it is dead, and Python raises nothing to tell you.

Guards decide what the pattern cannot

case [first, *rest] if first > 100:
    return f"spike at {first}, {len(rest)} more"

A guard is an if on the end of a case line, and it is Java's when under another spelling. The pattern runs first and binds its names, and the guard then reads those names and gives a yes or a no. A guard that says no does not end the match, so Python carries on to the next case and tries again.

That is why two cases can carry the same pattern with different guards. The first case whose guard holds is the one that wins, so put the narrow case above the broad one or the broad one will take everything.

A guard is an ordinary expression rather than part of the pattern, so it can compare two bound names, call a function, or read anything else in scope.

Your task

All three take untrusted input, so the parameters are annotated object where the tests send more than one type. Every one of them ends with case _.

  • summarise(samples) takes a list of whole numbers. An empty list gives "no samples". A list whose first sample is above 100 gives f"spike at {first}, {len(rest)} more", counting only what follows the first sample. A list of exactly one sample gives f"one sample: {only}". Any other list gives f"starts at {first}, {len(rest)} more". Anything that is not a list gives "not a batch".
  • axis(point) takes a pair of whole numbers as a list or a tuple. (0, 0) gives "origin". A zero second value gives f"on the x axis at {x}" and a zero first value gives f"on the y axis at {y}". A pair of equal values gives f"on the diagonal at {x}". Any other pair gives f"at {x},{y}". Anything that is not a pair gives "not a point".
  • setting(config) takes a dict. A "mode" of "auto" with a "limit" above 100 gives f"auto, limit {limit} above the safe band", and with any other limit gives f"auto up to {limit}". An "auto" mode with no limit key gives "auto with no limit". A "mode" of "manual" gives "manual, limit ignored". Any other mode gives f"unsupported mode {mode}", and a dict without a mode key gives "no mode given".

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not write if, elif or else as a statement. A guard on a case line is the only if these answers get.
  • Do not measure or index the subject. len(samples), point[0] and config["mode"] are all the pattern's job. len(rest) on a name the pattern bound is fine.
  • Do not call get and do not write in to test for a key. The mapping pattern does both.
  • Use no class pattern here. Lists, tuples and dicts only.
  • End every match with case _. A dispatch that falls off the end returns None in silence.
  • Annotate every signature, parameters and return alike.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI for explanation only. Ask it what an error means or why one form is more idiomatic. Do not let it write your answer.

question.answer:
def summarise(samples: object) -> str: match samples: case []: return "no samples" case [first, *rest] if first > 100: return f"spike at {first}, {len(rest)} more" case [only]: return f"one sample: {only}" case [first, *rest]: return f"starts at {first}, {len(rest)} more" case _: return "not a batch"
def axis(point: object) -> str: match point: case [0, 0]: return "origin" case [x, 0]: return f"on the x axis at {x}" case [0, y]: return f"on the y axis at {y}" case [x, y] if x == y: return f"on the diagonal at {x}" case [x, y]: return f"at {x},{y}" case _: return "not a point"
def setting(config: object) -> str: match config: case {"mode": "auto", "limit": limit} if limit > 100: return f"auto, limit {limit} above the safe band" case {"mode": "auto", "limit": limit}: return f"auto up to {limit}" case {"mode": "auto"}: return "auto with no limit" case {"mode": "manual"}: return "manual, limit ignored" case {"mode": mode}: return f"unsupported mode {mode}" case _: return "no mode given"

expected.text: no samples one sample: 42 spike at 200, 0 more spike at 150, 2 more starts at 3, 2 more not a batch

testcode.text: for point in [(0, 0), (5, 0), (0, -2), [3, 3], (2, 7), "ab", (1, 2, 3)]: print(axis(point)) for config in [{"mode": "auto", "limit": 50}, {"mode": "auto", "limit": 150}, {"mode": "auto", "limit": 50, "unit": "bar"}, {"mode": "auto"}, {"mode": "manual", "limit": 9}, {"mode": "burst"}, {"limit": 10}]: print(setting(config))

expected.text: origin on the x axis at 5 on the y axis at -2 on the diagonal at 3 at 2,7 not a point not a point auto up to 50 auto, limit 150 above the safe band auto up to 50 auto with no limit manual, limit ignored unsupported mode burst no mode given

import inspect
sources = {f.__name__: inspect.getsource(f) for f in (summarise, axis, setting)} for name, source in sources.items(): for line in source.splitlines(): head = line.strip() assert not head.startswith("if "), "rule broken: no if statement, a guard is the only if" assert not head.startswith("elif "), "rule broken: no elif in the dispatch" assert not head.startswith("else"), "rule broken: no else in the dispatch" assert "case _" in source, "rule broken: every match ends with case _" assert " if " in source, "rule broken: every answer carries a guard" assert "len(samples)" not in sources["summarise"], "rule broken: the pattern measures the list, not len" assert "samples[" not in sources["summarise"], "rule broken: do not index the subject" assert "*" in sources["summarise"], "rule broken: collect the rest with a starred name" assert "point[" not in sources["axis"], "rule broken: do not index the subject" assert "config[" not in sources["setting"], "rule broken: the mapping pattern reads the keys" assert ".get(" not in sources["setting"], "rule broken: do not call get, the pattern reads the keys" assert " in config" not in sources["setting"], "rule broken: do not test for a key with in" print(summarise([101]), "|", summarise([100, 1])) print(axis((-4, -4)), "|", axis([0, 0]), "|", axis([])) print(setting({"mode": "auto", "limit": 101}), "|", setting({})) print(setting(["mode", "auto"]))

questiontext.text:
Goal

Write three dispatchers that replace an isinstance ladder with one match statement each.

How this works in Python

Java 21 gave you a switch that reads a sealed hierarchy and takes records apart in the same line. You write the shape you expect, and the compiler checks you covered every permitted subtype.

sealed interface Event permits Reading, Alarm, Heartbeat {}
record Reading(String sensor, double value) implements Event {}

String classify(Event event) {
    return switch (event) {
        case Alarm a when a.status() == Status.FAILED -> "trip on " + a.code();
        case Reading(String sensor, double value) -> sensor + " reads " + value;
        case Heartbeat h -> h.node() + " is alive";
        default -> "unrecognised event";
    };
}

Before that arrived you wrote a ladder of instanceof tests with a cast in every branch. Python 3.10 added the same tool under the name structural pattern matching, spelled match and case. This is the closest thing in the language to that switch, and most Python tutorials predate it.

match event:
    case Reading(sensor=sensor, value=value):
        return f"{sensor} reads {value}"
    case _:
        return "unrecognised event"

Python runs the cases from the top and stops at the first one that fits. A match is a statement and not an expression, so each body returns or assigns rather than producing a value for the whole block. match and case are soft keywords, which means a variable called match elsewhere in your program keeps working.

Six kinds of pattern do the work. A literal pattern such as case 0: or case "stop": compares with ==. A capture pattern is a bare name. It matches anything and binds the subject to that name. case _: is the wildcard, which matches anything and binds nothing.

The capture pattern carries a trap worth its own sentence. A bare name in a case is a capture and never a comparison, so case FAILED: does not test the subject against your constant FAILED. It matches every subject, rebinds FAILED to whatever came in, and every case below it becomes dead code. Write a dotted name instead. case Status.FAILED: is a value pattern and compares, which is why enum members belong in a match and loose module constants do not.

A class pattern looks like a constructor call and does the work of instanceof plus the cast plus the field reads. case Reading(sensor=sensor, value=value): checks the type and binds the two attributes in one line. A dataclass also fills in __match_args__, so the positional form case Reading(sensor, value) works as well, and the keyword form is the one that survives somebody reordering the fields.

A guard is an if on the end of a case line. The pattern binds first and the guard then decides, so case Reading(sensor=sensor, value=value) if value > 100.0: reads the bound value. When the guard is false Python carries on to the next case.

A sequence pattern matches by length and position. case ["arm", node]: wants exactly two items and binds the second. A starred name collects the rest, so case ["log", *rest]: matches one item or a hundred. Strings and bytes never match a sequence pattern, which stops "arm" quietly matching a four-item list of characters.

A mapping pattern matches by key. case {"kind": "alarm", "code": code}: wants those two keys with that first value, and it ignores every other key in the dict. That subset rule is the opposite of the sequence rule, so read it twice.

Alternatives go in one case with |. case ["stop" | "halt"]: takes either word. Every alternative must bind the same names, so case [x] | [x, y]: is rejected.

Your task

Write three dispatchers over the supplied types. Leave the supplied block alone.

  • classify(event) takes a Reading, an Alarm or a Heartbeat. A failed alarm gives f"trip on {code}". Any other alarm gives f"alarm {code} is {status.value}". A reading above 100.0 gives f"{sensor} over range at {value}" and any other reading gives f"{sensor} reads {value}". A heartbeat gives f"{node} is alive". Anything else gives "unrecognised event".
  • route(command) takes a list of strings. An empty list gives "no command". ["stop"] and ["halt"] both give "stopping". ["arm", node] gives f"arming {node}". ["set", key, value] gives f"{key} set to {value}". A list starting with "log" gives f"log of {len(rest)} entries", counting only what follows the word. Anything else gives "unsupported command".
  • unpack(payload) takes a dict. A "kind" of "reading" with a string "sensor" and a float "value" gives f"reading {sensor}={value}". A "kind" of "alarm" with a "code" gives f"alarm {code}". Any other "kind" gives f"unsupported kind {kind}", and a dict without one gives "no kind given".

You pass when the printed output matches the expected text character for character.

Rules
  • Do not write isinstance anywhere. The match statement decides.
  • Do not write if, elif or else to choose a branch. A guard on a case line is the only if this answer gets.
  • Compare an enum member with a dotted name. case Status.FAILED compares, and case FAILED binds a new variable and eats every case below it.
  • Destructure in the pattern. An event.code inside a case body means the pattern did not do its job.
  • End every match with case _. A dispatch that falls off the end returns None in silence, and a silent None in a safety controller is a fault nobody reads.
Before you click Check

Write down what you expect each test to print. Then run it. A surprise means your model of Python is wrong, and that is the part worth learning.

AI protocol

AI allowed, on three conditions. Write your plan before you open it. Read every suggestion and reject the ones you did not plan. Type accepted code out yourself rather than pressing Tab.

testcode.text: events = [ Alarm("E17", Status.FAILED), Alarm("E18", Status.STALE), Reading("p1", 42.5), Reading("p2", 140.0), Heartbeat("node-a"), "not an event", ] for event in events: print(classify(event))

expected.text: trip on E17 alarm E18 is STALE p1 reads 42.5 p2 over range at 140.0 node-a is alive unrecognised event

print(trap(Status.OK)) print(trap(Status.STALE))
